To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) in an experiment that controlled for the possibility of experimental artefacts, we found that witnesses of unfairness do not punish on behalf of other people who have been treated unjustly; (2) in the same experiment we found that victims do punish on behalf of themselves, but not altruistically on behalf of other victims; (3) in a follow-up experiment that used an identical paradigm, we replicated the previous findings; and (4) previous evidence for altruistically punishing witnesses was likely

1) victims of unfairness, but not witnesses to unfairness, punish transgressors, 2) witnesses of unfairness feel envy rather than moralistic anger towards transgressors, and 3) previous experimental evidence for altruistic punishments plausibly resulted in part from affective forecasting errors.
(a) victims of unfairness punish unfair transgressors but witnesses of unfairness do not, and (b) witnesses of unfairness feel envy towards unfair individuals, not anger.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether human altruistic punishment is a genuine phenomenon.
the evolution of social norms and human cooperation, and the role of emotions in these processes.
altruistic punishment in the context of the evolution of cooperation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
humans do not punish altruistically.

the human species has evolved an adaptation for punishing on behalf of others, but only in the specific circumstances where the punisher has a chance of receiving a direct benefit via reciprocity or indirect benefits via kin selection.

the evidence for altruistic punishers in the sense that the term is commonly used is weak, but that the evidence for the existence of altruistic punishers as defined by the authors of the original studies is strong.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
humans are not as altruistically motivated as previously thought.
humans punish on behalf of others when they have a chance of benefiting themselves, but that they do not altruistically punish on behalf of other people when they have no such chance.
the altruistic punishment paradigm has not provided a good model for the study of human cooperation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
humans’ moral emotions can be complex.
we need to be more cautious about the conclusions we draw from laboratory experiments, particularly when the experimental design is vulnerable to artefacts.
we need to be more cautious when drawing inferences about the evolution of altruism from experimental data.
